newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says talks with Turkey centre on gas pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says talks with Turkey centre on gas pipeline.

text.p: Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Friday his talks with a visiting Turkish minister centred on building a strategic gas pipeline between the two countries.
"The gas pipeline project is as strategic as the Iraqi-Turkish oil pipeline set up during the 1980s," Rasheed said at the start of his talks with Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan.

The dual pipeline between the two countries is carrying the bulk of the $2 billion worth of Iraqi oil exports allowed by the United Nations in order to raise money to buy food and medicine for the sanctions-hit Iraqis.
The gas pipeline would be 1,300 km (800 miles) long and cost $2.5 billion. It could carry 10 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas a year.
Rasheed did not say when work would start in the gas project.
Iraq is under stringent U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The curbs ban foreign investment in Iraqi oil.
He said two agreements on the gas project were signed by the two countries, one in March 1996 and one in late 1995.
Rasheed said talks were progressing between Iraq and Turkey to develop a gas field and an oilfield which he did not name.
Turkish officials have previously named the gas field as al-Anfal, which came on stream in May 1990 at a rate of 200 million cubic feet a day.
Rasheed also said that Turkish firms would carry out oil exploration jointly with Iraq.

While Rasheed urged Ankara to enhance trade with Baghdad, Iraq's Foreign Minister Mohammad Saeed al-Sahaf strongly assailed Turkey for conducting joint military exercises with Israel and the U.S. in the Mediterranean.
"These manoeuvres are a military act against the Arabs and Moslems," Sahaf said in a statement carried by Iraqi newspapers on Friday.
"Iraq has the desire to renew its cross-border trade with Turkey as before the aggression (the 1991 Gulf War which ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait)," Rasheed said.
He said border trade used to reach $4 billion a year. Some 30,000 Turkish trucks were used to transport goods to Iraq every day and return with some 20 million litres of oil by-products annually.
